Explain every stage of the LNP model—linear filter, static nonlinearity, and conditional Poisson output—and why early vision is commonly modeled in terms of contrast rather than raw luminance.
Construct ON and OFF Difference-of-Gaussians receptive fields through spatial convolution and predict the response signs for a uniform field, a center spot, and surround illumination.

prerequisiteBridge: A receptive field is not merely an area of the screen; it is a relation between a stimulus pattern and a neural response. A linear spatial receptive field \(K(x,y)\) assigns a positive or negative weight to each location. Multiplying stimulus contrast \(s(x,y)\) by K everywhere and summing gives scalar drive L. Positive weights prefer bright contrast and negative weights prefer dark contrast, although the exact sign depends on the ON/OFF convention.

Define contrast as \(s=(I-I_{0})/I_{0}\), where I is local luminance and \(I_{0}\) is the adapted mean luminance. Division by \(I_{0}\) makes the same relative change comparable across background levels. A Poisson model converts a nonnegative rate r and time window T into the count distribution n~\(\operatorname{Poisson}(rT)\). It describes conditional variability and does not imply that real spikes are perfectly independent.

Only elementary trigonometry is needed for a two-dimensional rotation: \(x'=x \cos\theta +y \sin\theta\) and \(y'=y \cos\theta -x \sin\theta\). In the carrier \(\cos(kx'+\phi )\), k controls spatial angular frequency and \(\phi\) controls phase. After time is added, each stimulus history is an x-y-t volume. A moving edge traces an oblique line in the x-t plane whose slope is set by velocity.

modules.title: Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation
paragraphs: This lesson place photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), V1, MT, IT, and LIP on a hierarchy diagram. The retina first encodes local contrast; V1 emphasizes local structure such as orientation; MT and the dorsal stream are associated with motion and action-relevant variables; IT and the ventral stream with object features; and LIP often with decision-related representations. This course-level computational map does not imply exclusively one-way feedforward information flow.

Along the hierarchy, classical receptive fields generally become larger, the selected features more complex, and history dependence and context stronger. Higher-level cells may also become more invariant to position, phase, or local detail. Feature selectivity asks which stimulus pattern changes the response; a receptive field additionally asks which positions and time lags matter. A single heat-map color cannot capture both questions.

The LNP model has three ordered stages: linear, nonlinear, and Poisson. The linear stage \(L=K*s\) measures the match between a stimulus and a receptive-field template. The nonlinearity \(r=F(L)\) rectifies, thresholds, or saturates the drive to produce a plausible rate. Finally, n~\(\operatorname{Poisson}(rT)\) describes count variability conditional on the stimulus. LNP is descriptive; it does not claim that each stage occupies a separate anatomical box.

A Difference of Gaussians (DoG) often approximates an RGC center-surround receptive field. An ON-center filter subtracts a broad negative Gaussian from a narrow positive one; an OFF-center filter reverses every sign. If their integrals nearly balance, a uniform field cancels while center-surround differences are amplified. Threshold-linear rectification \([L]_{+}=\max(L,0)\) then separates ON and OFF drives into nonnegative feature maps.
keyPoints: The visual hierarchy mixes anatomy with computational abstraction; a region label is not an exclusive function.
An LNP linear drive may have either sign, the nonlinearity makes rate nonnegative, and a conditional distribution then generates spike count.
A DoG center-surround filter suppresses common luminance and highlights local contrast and edges.

derivation.title: From Contrast and Convolution to an ON-Center DoG
derivation.setup: Let \(r^2=x^2+y^2\) and define the normalized 2D Gaussian \(G_\sigma (r)=(2\pi \sigma ^2)^{-1}\exp[-r^2/(2\sigma ^2)]\), whose total integral is 1.

steps.title: Normalize Luminance First
steps.explanation: Use adaptation level \(I_{0}\) as baseline and define dimensionless contrast. When \(I=I_{0}\), \(s=0\); luminance above baseline is positive and luminance below it is negative.

steps.title: Define a Translated Receptive-Field Drive
steps.explanation: With cell center \((x_{0},y_{0})\) as reference, multiply the kernel by the stimulus at every position and integrate. Differences in the kernel arguments express the same receptive-field shape at different center locations.

steps.title: Construct Center-Surround and Test a Uniform Field
steps.explanation: Let \(K=A G_{\sigma _{c}}-B G_{\sigma _{s}}\), with \(\sigma _{s}>\sigma _{c}\). If \(A=B\), the integral of K is zero, so uniform contrast \(s_{0}\) gives \(L=s_{0}\int K=0\).

symbolNotes: \(\sigma _{c}\) and \(\sigma _{s}\) have units of spatial distance. A and B set integrated center and surround strength, not merely peak height.
K must have units such that K×area×contrast yields a linear drive. For discrete pixels, the integral becomes a sum that includes the pixel-area factor.
derivation.unitsCheck: Contrast is dimensionless. If x,y are measured in degrees of visual angle, a normalized Gaussian has units degree^{-2}, and integration leaves L with the drive units of A and B.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\sigma _{s}=\sigma _{c}\) and \(A=B\), the entire kernel is zero. If the surround is broad but B is not scaled for its area, comparing peak heights misrepresents total inhibitory strength.

workedExample.title: Predicting Signs in a Discrete Three-Position Center-Surround Filter
workedExample.problem: Use \(K=(-0.5,1,-0.5)\) for the left surround, center, and right surround. Compare stimuli \(s_{A}=(0,1,0)\) and \(s_{B}=(1,1,1)\), then rectify.
steps: \(L_{B}=-0.5+1-0.5=0\); the balanced kernel cancels uniform contrast.
With the OFF-center kernel -K, stimulus A gives -1 and therefore 0 after [L]_+.
workedExample.result: The ON-center filter has positive drive for a local bright spot and no linear drive for a uniform bright field; the OFF-center channel is suppressed by that same bright spot.
workedExample.sanityCheck: A zero sum of kernel weights is exactly the discrete condition for uniform cancellation. A nonzero sum leaves a residual response to a uniform field.

pitfalls: Treating a receptive field as a purely geometric boundary without defining its internal positive and negative weights, time lags, and response measure.
Comparing Gaussian centers and surrounds only by peak height while ignoring width, integrated strength, and the kernel sign convention.

modules.title: Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning
paragraphs: Convolving one kernel over all retinal locations produces a feature map. Each map pixel records how well the surrounding image patch matches the feature template; it is not the original image intensity. ON and OFF kernels yield two polarity-specific maps, and rectification retains positive drive for each filter's preferred polarity. This resembles shared filters in convolutional neural networks mathematically, but it does not make biological wiring, learning rules, or boundary treatment identical.

V1 simple-cell receptive fields often contain alternating elongated ON and OFF lobes. A Gabor kernel uses a Gaussian envelope to localize position and size and a cosine carrier to create the alternating lobes. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinates, k controls spatial frequency, and \(\phi\) controls phase. Orientation tuning arises because positive contributions add when an edge aligns with the lobes, whereas an orthogonal edge straddles positive and negative regions and cancels.

Changing \(\theta\) rotates the preferred orientation. Changing \(\phi\) translates the bright-dark lobe pattern along the carrier direction without changing orientation or frequency. Increasing k packs more lobes into each unit distance. Collapsing all three parameters into a single “direction” label prevents predictions about phase reversal or different bar widths.

A rectifying, saturating nonlinearity can turn linear Gabor drive into firing rate, for example \(r=r_{\mathrm{max}}[L]_{+}^2/(\alpha ^2+[L]_{+}^2)\). The response rises for small positive L, approaches \(r_{\mathrm{max}}\) for large L, and clips negative L. Localized sinusoidal analysis is mathematically related to wavelets and JPEG because all represent images with local scale-orientation components; this does not mean cortex implements the same codec.
keyPoints: Each location in a feature map stores a filter response, not a copy of the input image.
For a Gabor filter, the envelope sets localization, \(\theta\) sets orientation, k sets frequency, and \(\phi\) sets phase.
The nonlinearity determines sign handling, threshold, and saturation, so a single linear kernel can produce different tuning amplitudes.

derivation.title: How a Rotated Gabor Filter Produces Orientation-Selective Drive
derivation.setup: Start with coordinates (x,y) and use \(\theta\) to define carrier-aligned coordinates. Different Gaussian widths \(\sigma _{x}\),\(\sigma _{y}\) create an elongated envelope.

steps.title: Rotate the Coordinate System
steps.explanation: x' runs along the preferred carrier normal and y' is perpendicular to it. Rotation preserves distance and stimulus content; it changes only the coordinate basis.

steps.title: Write the Localized Carrier
steps.explanation: The Gaussian restricts the filter to a finite region, while the cosine generates alternating positive and negative lobes within it. Normalization can be chosen for the application.

steps.title: Explain the Tuning
steps.explanation: For a grating with matching k,\(\theta\),\(\phi\), regions of equal sign overlap and the inner product is large. A phase difference of \(\pi\) reverses the linear response; rectification can therefore make the two firing responses different.

symbolNotes: k is measured in radians per spatial distance, and cycles per degree equals \(k/(2\pi )\). Whether \(\theta\) names the grating's bar orientation or differs from it by 90° depends on whether orientation is defined by the wave-vector normal or the bar axis.
\(\phi\) is in radians and changes ON/OFF lobe alignment. \(\sigma _{x}\),\(\sigma _{y}\) use the same spatial units as x,y.
derivation.unitsCheck: Both kx' and \(\phi\) must be dimensionless, so k has units inverse distance. The exponential argument \(x'^2/\sigma _{x}^2\) is dimensionless as well.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(\sigma _{x}\),\(\sigma _{y}\to \infty\), localization is lost. As \(k\to 0\), the carrier approaches a constant and the kernel resembles a Gaussian blob rather than an oriented alternating filter.

workedExample.title: Simple-Cell Responses at One Orientation and Different Phases
workedExample.problem: Idealize the linear drive to a matching grating as \(L=A \cos(\phi _{s}-\phi _{K})\), with \(A=10\). Compare phase differences 0, \(\pi /2\), and \(\pi\) using \(r=[L]_{+}\).
workedExample.result: Simple-cell firing depends on both orientation/frequency matching and alignment of the light-dark phase.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Without rectification, the response at phase \(\pi\) is -10 rather than no response; nonnegativity of firing rate comes from the nonlinear stage.

pitfalls: Confusing the grating wave-vector direction with bar orientation without noting that they usually differ by 90°.
Treating rectification or saturation as part of the linear receptive field rather than distinguishing linear drive L from firing rate r.

modules.title: Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation
paragraphs: After time is included, the linear drive integrates past stimulus history: \(K(x',y',\tau )\) multiplies \(s(x-x',y-y',t-\tau )\), with \(\tau \ge 0\) denoting look-back time. Temporal lobes may be biphasic so that sustained components of a static image cancel. Because center and surround can have different time courses, an RGC receptive field is commonly nonseparable.

Every time slice of a separable kernel \(K(x,y,t)=K_{s}(x,y)K_{t}(t)\) has the same spatial pattern, differing only by a scalar amplitude. It can express a fixed-location feature that excites and then inhibits, but it cannot move the preferred location. In a nonseparable kernel, positive and negative lobes shift with lag, binding spatial position to temporal order.

A vertical edge moving rightward at velocity v satisfies \(x(t)=x_{0}+vt\). In an x-t diagram it is an oblique line of slope \(dx/dt=v\). If the positive lobes of a receptive field lie along the same line, the edge traverses every positive zone in sequence and produces a large inner product. An edge moving the other way follows the opposite slope and encounters mismatched positive and negative zones.

A rightward-motion receptive field has precisely this tilted pattern. Direction selectivity can also be built from multiple filters, quadratic motion energy, or recurrence, so a tilted linear receptive field is a testable minimal description. Eye movements, coordinate transformations, and finite display refresh alter the stimulus trajectory; experiments must state the reference frame.
keyPoints: Spatiotemporal convolution uses past stimulus history, so the orientation of the time-lag axis must be explicit.
A separable kernel's spatial profile does not move with lag; a tilted nonseparable kernel can encode the sign of velocity.
Motion is an orientation in the x-t plane, and velocity corresponds to trajectory slope.

derivation.title: The Matching Condition for a Moving Edge and a Tilted Receptive Field
derivation.setup: Ignore y and concentrate moving-edge contrast at \(x=x_{0}+vt\). Let a receptive-field ridge be concentrated at \(x=x_{c}-v\tau\), where \(\tau\) is a past lag.

steps.title: Write the Edge Position in the History
steps.explanation: Looking back by lag \(\tau\) from current time t places the edge at time \(t-\tau\) and position \(x_{0}+v(t-\tau )=x_{0}+vt-v\tau\), so its history trajectory has slope -v with respect to lag.

steps.title: Align the Edge with the Receptive-Field Ridge
steps.explanation: If the receptive-field ridge follows \(x=x_{c}-v\tau\) and \(x_{c}=x_{0}+vt\), the edge falls on the positive ridge at every lag, so all contributions add with the same sign.

steps.title: Reverse Direction to Produce a Mismatch
steps.explanation: Changing velocity to -v gives history trajectory \(x_{0}-vt+v\tau\). Its slope reverses, it no longer overlaps the original ridge, and it may cross inhibitory lobes.

symbolNotes: \(\tau\) is a nonnegative look-back time, not absolute clock time. If a receptive-field plot places the past above rather than below, the visible slope sign changes with the plotting convention.
v has units spatial distance/time, such as degree/s; x and receptive-field position must use the same spatial reference frame.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(v\tau\) has distance units and can be added to x. The spatiotemporal integral also includes dx \(d\tau\), so kernel normalization must preserve the drive units.
derivation.limitCheck: At \(v=0\) the ridge is untilted and selects a static feature. With an extremely short temporal window, opposite-direction trajectories have not separated enough and direction discrimination weakens.

workedExample.title: Matching a Discrete Three-Frame Trajectory
workedExample.problem: Across frames at times t-2,t-1,t, a rightward edge occupies positions 0,1,2. Put the receptive field's positive positions at 0,1,2 for the corresponding lags. Award +1 for a match and 0 otherwise; compare this sequence with leftward positions 2,1,0.
steps: The rightward sequence matches at all three lags, giving total linear drive \(1+1+1=3\).
The leftward sequence matches only at middle position 1; the other two frames mismatch, so total drive is 1.
With threshold 2, the rightward response passes and the leftward response is clipped to 0.
workedExample.result: The same three positions produce different responses when their temporal order differs; direction selectivity arises from a space-time conjunction.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If the three frames are averaged without order, both sequences contain positions \({0,1,2}\), and the distinction disappears. Temporal order is therefore indispensable.

pitfalls: Mixing time lag with absolute time, thereby flipping the receptive field on the temporal axis and reversing the inferred preferred direction.
Explaining motion tuning from a single-frame spatial receptive field without checking the joint pattern across positions and lags.

synthesis: The visual hierarchy is not merely an anatomical list but a computational organization in which receptive-field size, feature complexity, history dependence, and invariance change by stage. LNP first projects a stimulus onto a linear receptive field, maps the drive through a nonlinearity to a rate, and uses a Poisson process to describe spikes. DoG, Gabor, and nonseparable spatiotemporal kernels summarize center-surround, orientation, and motion selectivity.

commonTraps: Treating a receptive field only as a geometric region in visual space.
Using raw luminance and contrast interchangeably.
Leaving the sign or flip convention of a convolution kernel unstated.
Assuming a feature map is a copy of the original image rather than a map of filter responses.
Confusing Gabor orientation, phase, and spatial frequency.
Assuming a separable spatiotemporal receptive field is automatically direction-selective.
Equating an anatomical hierarchy with one purely feedforward computation.

Do not describe a receptive field only as a screen “location”; it is a stimulus-response relationship. Distinguish a linear receptive field, classical receptive field, and experimental definition. Sparse-noise receptive-field mapping provides a useful transfer example.

questions.explanation: This lesson place photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), V1, MT, IT, and LIP on a hierarchy diagram. The retina first encodes local contrast; V1 emphasizes local structure such as orientation; MT and the dorsal stream are associated with motion and action-relevant variables; IT and the ventral stream with object features; and LIP often with decision-related representations.
